findings 1 and 2 (do not start a server; do not touch pipeline/, data/, public/).

node scripts/check-secrets.mjs --all. Append "### Fix round 1" under the Muse
review section in docs/reviews/12.md listing what changed, and commit.

1|# Review: task 12, music session and one selection path
2|
3|## Grok Bot review
4|
5|Baseline on origin/main 7e4683f: 237 tests in 27 files. Branch after the
6|implementation run: 253 tests in 28 files, typecheck, check:size,
7|check:isolation, test:hooks, check-secrets --all and gitleaks all clean.
8|
9|Part 2 (one selection path) reads right: `audibleTracks` is the only
10|`playlistOnly !== true` filter, `compareTrackId` the only id tie-break,
11|`rankScored` scores each track once, and `selectScheduled` owns tolerance,
12|keep-current and the min-track hold. `noteTrackEnded` checks the empty
13|style before excluding the ended id, and `bestRanked` returns null on an
14|empty eligible set, so the outcome is the same as before.
15|
16|Findings:
17|
18|1. Must. The rng call order changed. Before, `evaluateRandom` drew first
19|   (`pickRandomTrack` called `rng()`) and applied the min-track hold
20|   afterwards. `selectScheduled` now returns early under the hold, before
21|   it draws. The visible pick is the same, but a seeded rng now advances
22|   differently during a hold, and the brief asked for identical rng
23|   consumption. Fix: draw first, then apply the hold to a pick that is
24|   not the current track.
25|2. Should. `canSkip` now comes from the view built at dispatch time with
26|   the route signal of that moment. Before, it was recomputed on every
27|   render from `routeSceneId`. Between a route change and the next
28|   dispatch (sceneEntered or the 1 s tick), the button can be stale for
29|   up to one tick. Either confirm sceneEntered always follows a route
30|   change in the same effect pass, or note the bound in the contracts doc.
31|
32|## Muse review, round 1
33|
34|What this change does: every music decision moves out of `app/reader.tsx`
35|into pure `core/music-session.ts` behind `startSession`/`dispatch`, and
36|the pick path collapses into one scope filter (`audibleTracks`), one
37|tie-break (`compareTrackId`), one scorer (`rankScored`), and one draw
38|(`selectScheduled`). The reader keeps routing, fetch, prefs, volume/mute,
39|and the `Player` markup. Checked by reading both versions of every
40|touched file, running the suite (28 files, 253 tests, all green with no
41|existing test edited), a scratch rng-count probe, and greps for leftover
42|refs, secrets, and new routes.
43|
44|Grok finding 1 (rng order): verified, kept below as finding 1.
45|Grok finding 2 (canSkip stale up to one tick): refuted as stated, see
46|finding 3. Every route change fires `sceneEntered` in the same effect
47|pass (`app/reader.tsx:121`, gated by observed-vs-route id), which rebuilds
48|the view with the fresh route signal. No contracts note needed.
49|
50|1. Must. Seeded rng diverges during the min-track hold
51|   (`core/music-selection.ts:102-107`).
52|   - What this is: the old `evaluateRandom` drew first (`rng()` inside
53|     `pickRandomTrack`) and applied the hold after, discarding the pick.
54|     `selectScheduled` returns before the draw while the hold is active.
55|   - Problem: the audible pick is the same (no switch either way), but a
56|     seeded rng advances once per hold under the old code and zero times
57|     now. Every later draw then picks a different track. My probe:
58|     hold-active draw consumes 0 `rng()` calls; the old order consumed 1.
59|     The spec demands identical rng consumption.
60|   - Fix: draw first, then hold, keeping a pick that is not the current
61|     track (exactly what Grok proposed). One or two lines in
62|     `selectScheduled`.
63|   - If we skip it: deterministic playback drifts from `origin/main`
64|     after any hold, and no test can pin the sequence.
65|2. Should. No test pins rng consumption, so finding 1 can come back.
66|   - What this is: `core/music-session.test.ts` uses a constant
67|     `rng: () => 0`, which cannot tell draw-first from hold-first apart.
68|   - Problem: the one behavior the refactor most easily breaks (call
69|     order with identical visible picks) has no failing test.
70|   - Fix: one test with a counting rng asserting one call per draw and
71|     the agreed hold-path count after finding 1 lands.
72|   - If we skip it: the next refactor reorders the draw again silently.
73|3. Nit. `canSkip` is cached at dispatch instead of per render, so it can
74|   lag one pre-effect render after a route change (old code read the new
75|   route id during that render). Same-effect `sceneEntered` corrects it
76|   before paint matters. No action; recorded only to close Grok finding 2.
77|
78|Also verified, no findings: switch rules, history push (all automatic
79|switches) vs no-push (Previous), replay-nonce wrap, single entry dwell,
80|tick pending-vs-route scene choice, Previous in playlist mode (nonce bump,
81|no history walk), style guard plus persist on selection identity only,
82|trackEnded excluding the ended id with the same empty-style outcome,
83|playlist enter/exit/first-track/wrap/one-track nonce, `canPrev`, and the
84|identical-object tick all match `origin/main`. Ranking order, ties, and
85|the non-hold draw are identical; `pickRandomTrack` keeps its null-scene
86|id cycle and delegates the rest. Contracts match the code. `check:size`
87|is clean, no secrets or raw client errors, no new endpoints, and
88|`pipeline/`, `data/`, `public/` are untouched (empty diff).
89|
90|Not checked: on-screen render (no server per instructions); the 237-test
91|baseline count, taken from the Grok review (the green suite plus zero
92|edits to existing tests cover the no-regression claim).
93|
94|Verdict: changes needed

# Durable Test Collateral

Verification is part of the delivered project when it can prevent the same
behavior from breaking again. Use the project's existing framework and
conventions.

Loading this skill does not mean the current turn asked for the change. While you
are still investigating — explaining existing behavior, or answering a design
question the user raised — use commands that only read and leave the repository
unmodified, tests included.

## Scale to the task

Skip the failing-test-first workflow below when the change is tiny and leaves
program logic alone (a typo, a text or style tweak, a config value, or a version
pin), when the work is a throwaway prototype or a standalone one-file script or
page, when the request adds features to a project you created earlier in this
session, or when the user asks for speed or a quick result. A quick direct check
of the changed behavior is enough there; if you add no maintained test, say so in
the report. A user request for tests anywhere in the session, or a
specification that makes tests a deliverable, still applies.

Any other bug fix or behavior change keeps the workflow at its smallest: one
focused failing test, the fix, that test passing, and, when a broad run is
required, one broad run after the final edit. A report that something already
built behaves wrongly is a bug fix, even when it comes with feature requests.

Before a test run that may take more than a minute or two, tell the user in one
line what runs and why. If you poll it, post a short status line between polls;
never poll a long run silently.

## Keep the check with the project

For a bug fix or behavior change, add or update the smallest maintained test in
the repository's normal test layout that exercises the changed behavior. If a
specification makes a reusable suite or test category a deliverable, implement
that suite instead of treating it as private verification.

An inline interpreter command, heredoc, scratch script, temporary-directory
test, demo, or manual probe may help diagnose the problem, but it does not
replace the maintained test. Keep a useful self-authored test unless the user
explicitly asks for a disposable probe.

Do not add a new test framework solely to satisfy this skill. If the repository
has no maintained harness and the request does not require one, disclose when
durable coverage would be disproportionate or infeasible and use the narrowest
honest verification instead.

On a later turn, update the maintained test even when the old suite remains
green and the user does not repeat the test request. Cover the new behavior,
not merely an unrelated cleanup in the test file.

## Prove the maintained check

Observe the authentic failure before the implementation change when it is safe
and runnable. Then make the smallest implementation change and run the focused
maintained test after the final relevant source or test edit.

Do not weaken or delete a real failing test to obtain green. Fix the product,
or explain why the test's expectation is wrong before changing that
expectation. Do not repeat an unchanged check solely to collect evidence.

Run a broad or full suite only when the user, a repository gate, or
proportionate risk requires it, and then once, after the final edit, rather
than after each intermediate edit. A focused regression test comes first; broad
proof does not substitute for missing focused coverage.

Before deciding what a repository gate requires, read what the repository
declares it runs: its CI workflow, its test entry points, and its root-level
scripts listed with hidden entries included. A suite the project itself runs
over this change is a gate, not an optional extra, and a suite that skips
itself when its data is absent is not a green result.

A runner is unavailable only after you tried to make it available. When the
repository ships the command that fetches or builds the missing fixture,
corpus, or toolchain, run that command once and then run the gate. Report the
gate unavailable only when that attempt itself failed, and say what failed.

If the real runner is unavailable but the focused test can still be authored
honestly, leave the focused test in the repository and say it was not run. Do
not fabricate a passing result.

</skill-body>
</read-skill-result>
